label: none

sentence: There are in total 14 such input categorical variables.
label: none

sentence: The categories in these variables need to be represented as numerical so that they (Meng and Xing, 2022)can be given as input to various machine learning algorithms.
label: none

sentence: Numerical representation is necessary so that machine learning algorithms can process categorical data effectively. 76 4.5.1 Dummy Encoding One-hot encoding technique is also known as the process of creating dummy variables.
label: none

sentence: By using this technique, categorical variables are transformed into binary vectors and each category is represented by a binary indicator (0 or 1) (Meng and Xing, 2022).
label: none

sentence: Every category present in a categorical variable becomes a separate variable (or feature) in the dataset.
label: none

sentence: Thus, if there are k categories in a categorical variable, k resultant columns get added to the dataset.
label: none

sentence: This is a disadvantage as it leads to a ‘Dummy Variable Trap’ (Mukherjee et al., 2022).
label: none

sentence: Instead, the dummy encoding technique helps to avoid the ‘Dummy Variable Trap’ as only k-1 variables are created from k categories in a variable (Mukherjee et al., 2022).
label: none

sentence: This conversion helps to interpret each category’s impact on the predictions done by the model.
label: none

sentence: This approach has been considered for this dataset even in the previous study, as Griffith et al., 2020 have mentioned the adjusted odds ratios for the relevant variables associated with mortality in their research paper.
label: none

sentence: Dummy variables are created by using the get_dummies() method in Python.
label: none

sentence: The dataset and the columns to be dummy encoded are given as parameters in this method.
label: none

sentence: There is another parameter ‘drop_first’ which is by default set to ‘False’.
label: none

sentence: If this parameter is set to ‘True’ it drops the first level and thus k-1 resultant columns get added for k categories.
label: none

sentence: But in this study, this parameter is kept as the default value (false) to manually select the dummy columns to be dropped rather than dropping the first dummy column.
label: none

sentence: Detecting Arbitrary Order Beneficial Feature Interactions for Recommender Systems Yixin Su yixins1@student.unimelb.edu.au The University of Melbourne Australia Yunxiang Zhao zhaoyx1993@163.com Bejing Institute of Biotechnology China Sarah Erfani∗ sarah.erfani@unimelb.edu.au The University of Melbourne Australia Junhao Gan junhao.gan@unimelb.edu.au The University of Melbourne Australia Rui Zhang rayteam@yeah.net www.ruizhang.info, China ABSTRACT Detecting beneficial feature interactions is essential in recommender systems, and existing approaches achieve this by examining all the possible feature interactions.
label: none

sentence: However, the cost of examining all the possible higher-order feature interactions is prohibitive (ex- ponentially growing with the order increasing).
label: research_gap

sentence: Hence existing approaches only detect limited order (e.g., combinations of up to four features) beneficial feature interactions, which may miss bene- ficial feature interactions with orders higher than the limitation.

label: none

sentence: To achieve an effective algorithm, we exploit three properties of beneficial feature interactions, and propose deep- infomax-based methods to guide the interaction generation.
label: none

sentence: Our experimental results show that HIRS outperforms state-of-the-art algorithms by up to 5% in terms of recommendation accuracy.

sentence: ACM, New York, NY, USA, 11 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3534678. 3539238 1 INTRODUCTION Features interactions (e.g., co-occurrence of user/item attributes) are essential in providing accurate recommendation predictions [3].
label: none

sentence: Pairwise feature interactions, as the most basic feature interac- tion form, have been utilized in many studies [14, 21, 34].
label: none

sentence: Recently, researchers found that more sophisticated forms of feature inter- actions (i.e., high-order interactions) help achieve more accurate recommendation predictions [23, 25].
label: none

sentence: For example, if we observe that male teenagers like Nolan’s sci-fi movies, the interactions (order-4) between user gender, user age, movie director, and movie genre provide useful information for recommendation that pairwise feature interactions cannot.
label: none

sentence: Since the number of all the possible feature interactions grows exponentially as the order increases, considering all the possible high-order feature interactions is prohibitive due to the high com- plexity.
label: research_gap

sentence: Meanwhile, considering the feature interactions irrelevant to the recommendation result may introduce noise and decrease the prediction accuracy [26, 40].
label: none

sentence: Therefore, a practical solution to con- sider high-order feature interactions is to detect a small set of most beneficial feature interactions and perform predictions based on the beneficial ones [44].
label: none

sentence: A set of feature interactions is considered most beneficial if learning from them results in a more accurate prediction than learning from other sets [33].
label: none

sentence: However, existing interaction detection methods have to examine all the possible fea- ture interactions to find the most beneficial feature interactions [25, 33].
label: research_gap

sentence: This leaves the complexity issue unsolved and they resort to detecting only limited order (e.g., combinations of up to four features) beneficial feature interactions (Figure 1 left).
label: research_gap

sentence: Hence, it is still an urgent yet challenging problem to efficiently detect arbitrary order beneficial feature interactions.
label: research_gap

sentence: In this work, we propose a method that can efficiently detect ben- eficial feature interactions of arbitrary orders.
label: none

sentence: Our method learns a neural network that directly generates the beneficial feature interac- tions (Figure 1 right).
label: none

sentence: The number of generated feature interactions can be specified to be much smaller than the number of all the arXiv:2206.13764v1 [cs.IR] 28 Jun 2022 Figure 1: Left: existing studies detect beneficial feature interactions within limited orders by examining all the possible feature inter- actions.
label: none

sentence: Right: we detect arbitrary order beneficial feature inter- actions by directly generating them with our deep-infomax-based methods (s-Infomax and Infomin). possible interactions and hence, our method admits a much lower running time.
label: none

sentence: Then, we achieve recommendation predictions based on the generated feature interactions.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, we propose a hy- pergraph neural network based model called Hypergraph Infomax Recommender System (HIRS).
label: none

sentence: HIRS learns a hypergraph representa- tion for each data sample, with each feature in the data represented as a node and each beneficial feature interaction represented as a hyperedge.
label: none

sentence: The beneficial feature interaction generation is con- ducted via hyperedge matrix prediction, and the recommendation prediction is conducted via hypergraph classification.
label: none

sentence: To achieve an effective beneficial feature interaction generation, we exploit three properties of beneficial feature interactions based on information theory: • Sufficiency: all beneficial feature interactions together contain as much relevant information about the true output as possible. • Low redundancy: each beneficial feature interaction contains as less irrelevant information about the true output as possible. • Disentanglement: any two beneficial feature interactions contain as less duplicated relevant information about the true output as possible.
label: none

sentence: Based on these properties, we leverage Deep Infomax [15] and pro- pose supervised mutual information maximization (s-Infomax) and mutual information minimization (Infomin) methods, together with an 𝐿0 activation regularization, to guide the interaction generation.
label: none

sentence: To effectively learn from the generated beneficial feature inter- actions for recommendation, we leverage the arbitrary-order cor- relation reasoning ability of hypergraph neural networks [9].
label: none

sentence: We propose an interaction-based hypergraph neural network (IHGNN) to perform recommendation prediction based on the generated interactions via hypergraph classification.
label: none

sentence: We summarize our contributions as follows: • We propose a hypergraph neural network based model named HIRS. 1.
label: none

sentence: HIRS is the first work that directly generates a set of beneficial feature interactions of arbitrary orders via hyperedge prediction and then performs recommendation prediction via hypergraph classification. • We define three properties of beneficial feature interactions to guide the proposed s-Infomax and Infomin methods for beneficial feature interaction generation.
label: none

sentence: We further propose an interaction- based hypergraph neural network (IHGNN), which effectively learns from the generated interactions for recommendation. 1The implementation of our model can be found at https://github.com/ruizhang- ai/HIRS_Hypergraph_Infomax_Recommender_System.git. • Experimental results show that HIRS outperforms state-of-the- art feature interaction based models for recommendation.
label: none

sentence: The further evaluations prove our model’s ability in beneficial feature interaction generation. 2 RELATED WORK 2.1 Feature Interaction based Recommendation Pairwise feature interactions have been widely used for recommen- dation, such as factorization machine (FM) based models [14, 28, 32] and graph neural network based models [21, 33].
label: none

sentence: Higher-order fea- ture interactions provide more information about the true output but have not been largely explored due to its high complexity.
label: research_gap

sentence: A multilayer perceptron (MLP) can implicitly model any order feature interactions for recommendation [6, 12, 16], but implicit modeling is ineffective in learning feature interactions [2].
label: research_gap

sentence: Lian et al. [23] explicitly model all feature interactions under a limited order (e.g., up to four orders).
label: none

sentence: Besides modeling all feature interactions, there are studies that detect a set of beneficial feature interactions for recommendation [25, 33].
label: none

sentence: However, they have to examine all the possible feature interactions, which leaves the complexity issue unsolved.
label: research_gap

sentence: Different from existing studies, we directly generate ben- eficial feature interactions without examining all the possible ones. 2.2 Graph Neural Networks Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are powerful in correlation reason- ing between entities [43, 45].
label: none

sentence: They have been applied in various research domains such as molecular prediction [11], object relation learning [4], and user-item interaction modeling [36, 39].
label: none

sentence: Recently, GNNs show the power of feature interaction learning for recommen- dation [21, 22, 33].
label: none

sentence: However, existing studies only capture pairwise feature interactions in a graph since each edge can only link to two nodes.
label: research_gap

sentence: We are the first to capture arbitrary order feature interac- tions and propose a Hypergraph Neural Network [9] based model to learn arbitrary order feature interactions uniformly. 2.3 Mutual Information Maximization Mutual information maximization is a critical technique in unsu- pervised representation learning [24].
label: none

sentence: Deep Infomax (DIM, Hjelm et al. [15]) leverages a deep neural network-based method [1] to maximize the mutual information between an image’s local and global representations.
label: none

sentence: A graph-based DIM is proposed to maxi- mize the mutual information between node representations and graph representations [37].
label: none

sentence: For the first time, our work applies DIM on hypergraph that maximizes the mutual information between hyperedge representations and graph representations.
label: none

sentence: Contrastive learning is close to DIM but maximizes the mutual information between the two views of the same variable [5].
label: none

sentence: Tian et al. [35] define properties of good views in contrastive learning.
label: none

sentence: They hy- pothesize that each view contains all the information of an input variable about the output.
label: none

sentence: We define the properties of beneficial feature interactions hypothesizing that each interaction only con- tains part of the information about the output.
label: none

sentence: Khosla et al. [17] extend contrastive learning to a supervised setting.
label: none

sentence: Our s-Infomax is similar to [17] but applies the supervised learning between local and global representations. 3 PRELIMINARIES 3.1 Hypergraph Neural Networks Different from the edges in a typical graph, each edge in a hyper- graph (i.e., hyperedge) can link to an arbitrary number of nodes.
label: none

sentence: A hypergraph 𝐺𝐻= ⟨V, E⟩contains a node set V = {𝑖}𝑚 𝑖=1, where 𝑚is the number of nodes.
label: none

sentence: Each node 𝑖is represented as a vector 𝒗𝑖∈R𝑑of 𝑑dimensions (e.g., node embedding).
label: none

sentence: The hyperedge set E = {𝒆𝑗}𝑘 𝑗=1 contains 𝑘edges.
label: none

sentence: Each edge 𝒆𝑗is an 𝑚-dimensional binary vector (𝑒𝑗𝑖∈{0, 1}), where 𝑒𝑗𝑖= 1 if the 𝑗𝑡ℎedge links to node 𝑖, and 𝑒𝑗𝑖= 0 otherwise.

sentence: In general, Hypergraph Neural Network (HGNN, Feng et al. [9]) first generates a representation 𝒉𝑗for each hyperedge 𝑗by aggregating the linked node vectors.
label: none

sentence: Then, each node vector is updated by aggregating the edge representations linked to the node (called node patch representation).
label: none

sentence: The procedure is: 𝒉𝑗= 𝜙({𝑽𝑖|𝑬𝑖𝑗= 1}𝑖∈V), 𝒗′ 𝑖= 𝜓({𝒉𝑗|𝑬𝑖𝑗= 1}𝒆𝑗∈E), (1) where 𝜙(·) and 𝜓(·) are aggregation functions (e.g., element-wise mean), and 𝒗′ 𝑖is the patch representation of node 𝑖.
label: none

sentence: The graph representation 𝒄∈R𝑑can be generated by further aggregating the node patch representations: 𝒄= 𝜂({𝒗′ 𝑖}𝑖∈V), (2) where 𝜂(·) is an aggregation function similar to 𝜙(·) and 𝜓(·). 3.2 Deep Infomax Given two random variables 𝐴and 𝐵, Mutual Information Neural Estimation (MINE, Belghazi et al. [1]) estimates the mutual infor- mation 𝐼(𝐴; 𝐵) by training a discriminator that distinguishes the samples from their joint distribution J and from their marginal distribution M.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, MINE uses Donsker-Varadhan repre- sentation (DV, Donsker and Varadhan [8]) of KL-divergence as the lower bound to the mutual information: 𝐼(𝐴; 𝐵) = 𝐷𝐾𝐿(J||M) ⩾ˆ𝐼𝐷𝑉 𝜔 (𝐴; 𝐵) = EJ [𝑇𝜔(𝑎,𝑏)] −log EM [𝑒𝑇𝜔(𝑎,𝑏) ], (3) where 𝑎and 𝑏are the samples of 𝐴and 𝐵, respectively, and 𝑇𝜔is a classifier with parameters 𝜔.
label: none

sentence: In Deep Infomax [15] that aims to maximize a mutual informa- tion, the exact mutual information value is not important.
label: none

sentence: There- fore, ˆ𝐼𝐷𝑉 𝜔 (𝐴; 𝐵) can be conveniently maximized by optimizing a GAN-like objective function [20, 37]: L = EJ [log𝑇𝜔(𝑎,𝑏)] + EM [log(1 −𝑇𝜔(𝑎,𝑏))].
label: none

sentence: (4) This objective function can be optimized by training the discrim- inator 𝑇𝜔through a Binary Cross Entropy (BCE) loss [37]. 4 PROBLEM STATEMENT Denote by J the universe of features.

sentence: In this work, we present the Convolutional Reconstruction Model (CRM), a high-fidelity feed-forward single image-to-3D generative model.
label: none

sentence: Recognizing the limitations posed by sparse 3D data, we highlight the necessity of integrating geometric priors into network design.
label: none

sentence: CRM builds on the key observation that the visualization of triplane exhibits spatial correspondence of six orthographic images.
label: none

sentence: First, it generates six orthographic view images from a single input image, then feeds these images into a convolutional U-Net, leveraging its strong pixel-level align- ment capabilities and significant bandwidth to create a high-resolution triplane.
label: none

sentence: CRM further employs Flexicubes as geometric representation, facilitating direct end-to-end optimization on textured meshes.
label: none

sentence: Overall, our model delivers a high-fidelity textured mesh from an image in just 10 seconds, without any test-time optimization.

sentence: Keywords: 3D Generation · Textured Mesh · Diffusion Models 1 Introduction In recent years, generative models have witnessed significant advancements, largely attributed to the fast growth in data size.
label: none

sentence: Transformers [55], in partic- ular, have achieved high-performance results across various domains including language [3], image [1,37] and video generation [2].
label: none

sentence: However, the domain of 3D generation presents unique challenges.
label: research_gap

sentence: Unlike the abundance of other modal’s data, 3D data is comparatively scarce.
label: research_gap

sentence: The creation of 3D data requires special- ized expertise and considerable time, leading to a situation where the largest 3D datasets, namely Objaverse [12, 13], only contain millions of 3D content, much smaller than image datasets like Laion [45] which contains 5 billion images.
label: none

sentence: Despite this, recent developments have introduced some transformer-based methods [18, 21, 59, 63, 70] like LRM [18] for creating 3D content from single or multi-view images in a feed-forward manner.
label: none

sentence: Among these models, the tri- plane has emerged as a popular component due to its efficiency in generat- ing high-resolution 3D results with minimal memory cost.
label: none

sentence: However, reliance on transformer-based networks for generating triplane patches has not utilized the geometric priors inherent to the triplane concept, leading to sub-optimal results in terms of quality and fidelity, and long training time.
label: research_gap

sentence: To address the above challenges, this paper presents a new Convolutional Re- construction Model (CRM) with high generation quality as well as fast training.
label: none

sentence: Given the limited amount of 3D contents, CRM builds on a key hypothesis that it is beneficial to explore geometric priors in architecture design.
label: none

sentence: Namely, we observe from the visualization of triplane [5,6,47] that triplane exhibits spatial correspondence of input six orthographic images, as shown in Fig. 2.
label: none

sentence: The silhou- ette and texture of the input images have a natural alignment with the triplane structure.
label: none

sentence: This motivates us to (1) use six orthographic images as input images to reconstruct 3D contents, which align well as the triplane feature, instead of other arbitrarily chosen poses; (2) use a U-Net convolutional network to map the input images to a rolled-out triplane by exploring the strong pixel-level alignment Convolutional Reconstruction Model 3 between the input and output.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, the significant bandwidth capacity of our U-Net enables a direct transformation of the six orthographic images into the triplane, yielding highly detailed outcomes.
label: none

sentence: Besides, we also add Canonical Coordinate Map (CCM) to the reconstruction network, a novel addition that enriches the model’s understanding of spatial relations and geometry.
label: none

sentence: For the task of 3D generation from a single image, as the six orthographic images and CCMs are not directly available, we train a multi-view diffusion model conditioned on the input image to generate the six orthographic images and another diffusion model to generate the CCMs conditioned on the generated six orthographic images.
label: none

sentence: Both diffusion models are trained on a filtered version of the Objaverse dataset [13].
label: none

sentence: To further enhance quality and robustness, we implement training improvements for the multi-view diffusion models, including Zero-SNR [26], random resizing, and contour augmentation.
label: none

sentence: Finally, as directly optimizing high-quality textured meshes is challenging, we adopt Flexicubes [46] as the geometry representation to falicitate gradient-based mesh optimization.
label: none

sentence: This is unlike previous works [18,70] that use alternative 3D representation like NeRF [35] or Gaussian Splatting [19].
label: none

sentence: Such methods often involve extra procedure steps to obtain textured meshes [51], although they can produce detailed visualizations.
label: research_gap

sentence: With our designs, we are able to train CRM with textured mesh as the final output in an end-to-end manner, and our approach has a more straightforward inference pipeline and better mesh quality.
label: none

sentence: Overall, our method can generate high-fidelity textured mesh within 10 seconds, as shown in Fig. 1. 2 Related Works 2.1 Score Distillation for 3D Generation DreamFusion [38] proposes a technique called Score Distillation Sampling (SDS) (also known as Score Jacobian Chaining [56]).

sentence: Then we develop our convolutional reconstruction model (CRM, Sec. 3.2) to reconstruct 3D textured mesh from the images and CCMs. 3.1 Multi-view Diffusion Model We first explain the design of the multi-view diffusion model to generate six orthographic view images from a single input image.

label: none

sentence: To make the model insensitive to the contour, we randomly change the contour color during training. 3.2 Convolutional Reconstruction Model We now move to introduce the detailed architecture of the convolutional recon- struction model (CRM).
label: none

sentence: As outlined in Fig. 4, given the input six images and CCMs, a convolutional U-Net is used to map the input images along with the CCMs to a rolled-out triplane.
label: none

sentence: Then the rolled-out triplane is reshaped into the triplane.
label: none

sentence: Small multi-layer perceptions (MLPs) are used to decode the triplane features into SDF values, texture color and Flexicubes parameters.

sentence: Triplane Representation We choose triplane as the 3D representation, be- cause it can achieve high resolution 3D results with 2D computation consump- tion.
label: none

sentence: It projects each query grid cell to axis-aligned orthogonal planes (xy, xz, and yz planes) and then aggregates the feature from each planes.
label: none

sentence: Then the fea- ture is decoded by 3 tiny MLPs with 2 hidden layers to get the SDF values along with deformation, color and Flexicubes weights, respectively.
label: none

sentence: Further, to avoid the unnecessary entanglements of different planes, we use rolled-out triplane [60].
label: none

sentence: Canonical Coordinates Map (CCM) We also add CCM as input [22], which contains extra geometry information.
label: none

sentence: This is different from previous works, which typically use pure RGB images as the input to predict the 3D object [18].
label: none

sentence: Using pure RGB images make it extremely hard to predict the correct geometry, and sometime the geometry degrades (details in Sec. 4.3).
label: research_gap

sentence: Formally, CCM is the coordinates of each point in canonical space.
label: none

sentence: It contains 3 channels whose values are within [0, 1], representing the coordinates in the canonical space.
label: none

sentence: UNet-based Convolutional Network Our key insight is that the triplane is spatially aligned with the input six orthographic images and CCMs, as shown in Fig. 2.
label: none

sentence: To match the rolled-out triplane, the six images and CCMs are arranged in a similar way.
label: none

sentence: We render the six images and CCMs at a resolution of 256 × 256.
label: none

sentence: They are split into two groups, with each group holding three images.
label: none

sentence: These images in the four groups are then combined to create four larger images, each with a resolution of 256 × 768, allowing for spatial alignment.
label: none

sentence: By concatenating these four groups, we form a 12-channel input.
label: none

sentence: Next, a convolutional U-Net processes this input to produce the output triplane.
label: none

sentence: Compared to transformer-based methods [18,21,63,70], our U-shape design has a larger bandwidth in preserving the input information, leading to highly detailed triplane features and finally elaborate textured meshes.

sentence: POLICY DECORATOR: MODEL-AGNOSTIC ONLINE RE- FINEMENT FOR LARGE POLICY MODEL Xiu Yuan∗, Tongzhou Mu∗, Stone Tao, Yunhao Fang, Mengke Zhang, Hao Su UC San Diego {x1yuan, t3mu, stao, yuf026, mezhang, haosu}@ucsd.edu ABSTRACT Recent advancements in robot learning have used imitation learning with large models and extensive demonstrations to develop effective policies.
label: none

sentence: However, these models are often limited by the quantity, quality, and diversity of demonstrations.
label: research_gap

sentence: This paper explores improving offline-trained imitation learning models through online interactions with the environment.
label: none

sentence: We introduce Policy Decorator, which uses a model-agnostic residual policy to refine large imitation learning models during online interactions.
label: none

sentence: By implementing controlled exploration strategies, Policy Decorator enables stable, sample-efficient online learning.
label: none

sentence: Our evaluation spans eight tasks across two benchmarks—ManiSkill and Adroit—and involves two state-of-the-art imitation learning models (Behavior Transformer and Diffusion Policy).
label: none

sentence: The results show Policy Decorator effectively improves the offline-trained policies and preserves the smooth motion of imitation learning models, avoiding the erratic behaviors of pure RL policies.
label: none

sentence: Encouraged by the recent success of large language and vision foundation models (Brown et al., 2020; Kirillov et al., 2023), the field of robot learning has seen signif- icant advances through imitation learn- ing (particularly behavior cloning), where large models leverage extensive robotic demonstrations to develop effective poli- cies (Bousmalis et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2022; 2023; Ahn et al., 2022).
label: none

sentence: Despite these advancements, the performance of learned models is limited by the quan- tity, quality, and diversity of pre-collected demonstration data.
label: research_gap

sentence: This limitation often prevents models from handling all poten- tial corner cases, as demonstrations cannot cover every possible scenario (e.g., test- time objects can be entirely different from training ones).
label: research_gap

sentence: Unlike NLP and CV, scaling up demonstration collection in robotics, such as RT-1 (Brohan et al., 2022) and Open X-Embodiment (Collaboration, 2023), requires extensive time and resources, involving years of data collection by numerous human teleoperators, making it costly and time-consuming.
label: research_gap

sentence: In contrast, cognitive research indicates that infants acquire skills through active interaction with their environment rather than merely observing others (Saylor & Ganea, 2018; Sheya & Smith, 2010; Adolph et al., 1997; Corbetta, 2021).
label: none

sentence: This raises a natural question: Can we further improve an offline-trained large policy through online interactions with the environment?
label: none

sentence: The most straightforward approach to improving an offline-trained imitation learning policy is to fine-tune it using reinforcement learning (RL) with a sparse reward (Kumar et al., 2022; Yang et al., 2023a).
label: none

sentence: However, several challenges hinder this strategy.
label: none

label: none

sentence: Residual Policy (small, learnable) observation sparse reward action Controlled Exploration Evaluation Figure 2: Our framework (Policy Decorator) improves large policy models through online inter- actions.
label: none

sentence: We learn a residual policy via RL using controlled exploration strategies (Sec. 4.2).
label: none

sentence: Once learned, it functions similarly to Python decorators—wrapping the base policy with an additional function to boost performance. learning models have specific designs to accommodate the multimodal action distributions in the demonstrations, which unfortunately make them non-trivial to fine-tune using RL.
label: research_gap

sentence: For example, Behavior Transformer (Shafiullah et al., 2022), MCNN (Sridhar et al., 2023), and VINN (Pari et al., 2021) all incorporate some non-differentiable components (clustering, nearest neighbor search) which are incompatible with the gradient-based optimization in RL.
label: research_gap

sentence: Similarly, Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023) requires ground truth action labels to supervise its denoising process, but these action labels are unavailable in RL setups (refer to Appendix H.1 for a more detailed discussion).
label: research_gap

sentence: Secondly, even if an imitation learning model were compatible with RL, the fine-tuning process would be prohibitively costly for two reasons: 1) the increasing number of parameters in modern large policy models, and 2) the extensive gradient updates required during sparse-reward RL training, a process known for its poor sample efficiency.
label: research_gap

sentence: To devise a method for online improvement, we must first understand why an offline-trained imitation learning policy sometimes fails to solve tasks.
label: none

sentence: As studied in (Ross et al., 2011; Ross & Bagnell, 2010; Syed & Schapire, 2010; Chang et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2020), a major issue with policies learned from purely offline data is compounding error.
label: none

sentence: Small errors gradually accumulate, eventually leading the policy to states not covered in the demonstration dataset.
label: none

sentence: However, correcting these errors may only require minimal effort.
label: none

sentence: Even if the final trajectory deviates significantly from the correct path, slight adjustments can bring it back on track, as shown in Fig. 3.
label: none

sentence: In other words, the model only needs "refinement" for the finer parts of the tasks.
label: none

sentence: Modeling such small adjustments typically does not necessitate complex architectures or large numbers of parameters.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, we propose to online learn a residual policy (parameterized by a small network) to correct the behavior of the offline-trained imitation learning models, referred to as the "base policy" throughout this paper.
label: none

sentence: This approach addresses the incompatibility between models and RL and avoids the costly gradient updates on large models.
label: none

sentence: States Covered by Training Data = Goal One of the Demo Trajectory From Trained Policy Small Adjustment Figure 3: Small adjustments can bring deviated trajectories back on track.
label: none

sentence: While learning a residual policy through online RL (Jo- hannink et al., 2019; Alakuijala et al., 2021; Silver et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2019) can, in principle, refine a base policy, practical implementation is still challenging.
label: research_gap

sentence: As demonstrated in our experiments (Sec. 5), without con- straints, random exploration during RL training often leads to failure in tasks requiring precise control, resulting in no learning signals in sparse reward settings (see this video for an example).
label: none

sentence: To overcome these challenges and enable stable, sample-efficient learning, we propose a set of strategies to ensure the RL agent (with the residual policy) explores the environment in a controlled manner.
label: none

sentence: This approach ensures that the agent continuously receives sufficient success signals while adequately exploring the environment.
label: none

sentence: We call this framework the Policy Decorator because it functions similarly to decorators in Python—enhancing the original policy by wrapping it with an additional function to boost its performance, as illustrated in Fig. 2.
label: none

sentence: Like Python decorators, our framework does not require any prior knowledge of the original policy and treats it as a black box, making it model-agnostic.
label: none

sentence: We evaluate our approach across a variety of benchmarks and imitation learning models.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, we examine 8 tasks from 2 benchmarks: ManiSkill (Mu et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2023) and Adroit 2 (Rajeswaran et al., 2017), in conjunction with 2 state-of-the-art imitation learning models: Behavior Transformer (Shafiullah et al., 2022) (action clustering + regression) and Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023) (diffusion models + receding horizon control).
label: none

sentence: Our results demonstrate that the Policy Decorator consistently improves various offline-trained large policy models to near-optimal performance in most cases.
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, the learned policy maintains the desirable properties of the imitation learning policy, producing smooth motions rather than the jerky motions generated by pure RL policies.
label: none

sentence: To summarize, our contributions are as follows: • Conceptually, we raise the critical research question: "How can large policy models be improved through online interactions?", and identify limitations of fine-tuning and vanilla residual RL. • Technically, we propose Policy Decorator, a model-agnostic framework for refining large policy models through online environmental interactions. • Empirically, we conduct extensive experiments on 8 challenging robotic tasks and 2 state-of-the-art imitation learning models, demonstrating Policy Decorator’s advantages in both task performance and learned policy properties. 2 RELATED WORKS Learning from Demo Learning control policies through trial and error can be inefficient and unstable, prompting research into leveraging demonstrations to enhance online learning.
label: none

sentence: Demonstrations can be utilized through pure offline imitation learning, including behavior cloning (Pomerleau, 1988) and inverse reinforcement learning (Ng et al., 2000).
label: none

sentence: Alternatively, demonstrations can be incorporated during online learning, serving as off-policy experience (Mnih et al., 2015; Hessel et al., 2018; Ball et al., 2023; Nair et al., 2018) or for on-policy regularization (Kang et al., 2018; Rajeswaran et al., 2017).
label: none

sentence: Furthermore, demonstrations can be used to estimate reward functions for RL problems (Xie et al., 2018; Aytar et al., 2018; Vecerik et al., 2019; Zolna et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2019).
label: none

sentence: When the offline dataset includes both demonstrations and negative trajectories, offline-to-online RL approaches first apply offline RL to learn effective policy and value initializations from offline data, followed by online fine-tuning (Nair et al., 2020; Kostrikov et al., 2021; Lyu et al., 2022; Nakamoto et al., 2024).
label: none

sentence: In this work, we adopt a more direct approach to utilize demonstrations: distilling demonstrations into a large policy model and subsequently improving it through online interactions.
label: none

sentence: Residual Learning The concept of learning residual components has been widely applied across various domains, including addressing the vanishing gradient problem in deep neural networks (He et al., 2016; Vaswani, 2017) and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (Hu et al., 2021).
label: none

sentence: In robotic control, researchers have employed online RL to learn corrective residual components for various base policies, such as hand-crafted controllers (Johannink et al., 2019), non-parametric models (Haldar et al., 2023b), and pre-trained neural networks (Alakuijala et al., 2021; Ankile et al., 2024).
label: none

sentence: Residual learning can also be achieved through supervised learning (Jiang et al., 2024).
label: none

sentence: Our work focuses on the online improvement of large policy models, identifying residual policy learning as an ideal solution due to its model-agnostic nature.
label: none

sentence: We highlight the uncontrolled exploration issue in vanilla residual RL, propose a set of strategies to address it, and further enhance its efficiency through careful examination of design choices.
label: none

sentence: Advanced Imitation Learning Imitation learning provides an effective approach to teaching robots complex skills.
label: none

sentence: However, naive imitation learning often struggles to model multi-modal distributions within demonstration datasets (Chi et al., 2023).
label: research_gap

sentence: Several advanced methods have been proposed to address this limitation: Shafiullah et al. (2022); Lee et al. (2024); Sridhar et al. (2023); Pari et al. (2021) represent actions as discrete values with offsets, Florence et al. (2022) employs energy-based models, and Chi et al. (2023) leverages diffusion models.
label: none

sentence: While these techniques effectively learn from multi-modal data, they often create models that are non-trivial to fine-tune using RL.
label: research_gap

sentence: Even if they were compatible with RL, the fine-tuning process can be computationally prohibitive due to the large number of parameters in modern policy models.
label: research_gap

sentence: These limitations motivate our approach of using online residual policy learning to improve imitation learning models. 3 PROBLEM SETUP In this paper, we focus on improving an offline-trained large policy (referred to as "base policy") through online interactions.
label: none

sentence: We make the following assumptions: 3 1.
label: none

sentence: An environment is available for online interactions with task success signals (sparse rewards). 2.
label: none

sentence: The base policy may have a large number of parameters or complex architectures, making fine- tuning non-trivial or computationally expensive.
label: none

sentence: This assumption holds for many modern large policy models (Brohan et al., 2022; 2023; Chi et al., 2023; Shafiullah et al., 2022). 3.
label: none

sentence: The base policy exhibits reasonable initial performance, though not perfect (i.e., it can make progress towards task completion, which is achievable by many state-of-the-art IL methods with a reasonable amount of demonstrations).
label: limitation

sentence: An excessively poor base policy is not worth improving.
label: limitation

sentence: Note that our approach does not make any specific assumptions about model architectures or training methods.
label: none

sentence: Instead, we treat these models as black boxes that take observations as input and produce actions as output.
label: none

sentence: In our experiments, we choose to improve base policies trained by imitation learning rather than offline RL policies.
label: none

sentence: This is because: 1) collecting demonstrations alone is more cost-effective and thus more common; 2) as demonstrated in multiple studies (Mandlekar et al., 2021; Florence et al., 2022), imitation learning outperforms offline RL in demonstration-only settings. 4 POLICY DECORATOR: MODEL-AGNOSTIC ONLINE REFINEMENT In this work, our goal is to online improve a large policy model, which is usually offline-trained by imitation learning and usually has some specific designs in model architecture.
label: none

sentence: To this end, we propose Policy Decorator, a model-agnostic framework for refining large policy models via online interactions with environments.
label: none

sentence: Fig. 2 provides an overview of our framework.
label: none

sentence: Policy Decorator is grounded on learning a residual policy via reinforcement learning with sparse rewards, which is described in Sec. 4.1.
label: none

sentence: On top of it, we devise a set of strategies to ensure the RL agent (in combination with the base policy and the residual policy) explores the environment in a controlled manner.
label: none

sentence: Such a controlled exploration mechanism is detailed in Sec. 4.2.
label: none

sentence: Finally, we discuss several important design choices that further enhance learning efficiency in Sec. 4.3. 4.1 LEARNING RESIDUAL POLICY VIA RL Given the base policy πbase, we then train a residual policy πres on top of it using reinforcement learning.
label: none

sentence: The base policy πbase can be either deterministic (e.g., Behavior Transformer (Shafiullah et al., 2022)) or stochastic (e.g., Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023)), and it remains frozen during the RL process.
label: none

sentence: The residual policy πres is updated through RL gradients, so it should be a differentiable function compatible with RL gradients.
label: none

sentence: In this work, we model the residual policy πres as a Gaussian policy parameterized by a small neural network (either an MLP or a CNN, depending on the observation modality).
label: none

sentence: To interact with the environment, the actions from both policies are combined by summing their output actions, i.e., the action executed in the environment is πbase(s) + πres(s).
label: none

sentence: For stochastic policies, actions are sampled individually from both policies and then summed.
label: none

sentence: The residual policy is trained to maximize the expected discounted return derived from the sparse reward (i.e., the task’s success signal).
label: none

sentence: We employ the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) algorithm (Haarnoja et al., 2018) due to its superior sample efficiency and stability.
label: none

sentence: Several important design choices arise when implementing SAC for learning the residual policy, which we discuss in Sec. 4.3.
label: none

sentence: Our method is also compatible with PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), as illustrated in Appendix D.3. 4.2 CONTROLLED EXPLORATION While learning a residual policy by RL can in principle refine a base policy, practical implementation can be challenging.
label: none

sentence: As demonstrated in our experiments (Sec. 5), without constraints, random exploration during RL training often leads to failure in tasks requiring precise control, resulting in no learning signals in sparse reward settings (see this video for an example).
label: none

sentence: To overcome these challenges and enable stable, sample-efficient learning, we propose a set of strategies ensuring the RL agent (in combination with the base policy and the residual policy) explores the environment in a controlled manner.
label: none

sentence: The goal is to make sure the agent continuously receives sufficient success signals while adequately exploring the environment.
label: none

sentence: Bounded Residual Action When using the residual policy to correct the base policy, we do not want the resulting trajectory to deviate too much from the original trajectory because it usually leads to failure.
label: none

sentence: Instead, we expect the residual policy to only make a bit "refinement" at the finer parts of the 4 Figure 5: Tasks Visualizations.
label: none

sentence: ManiSkill (left four figures) and Adroit (right four figures). tasks.
label: none

sentence: To reflect this spirit, we bound the output of the residual policy within a certain scale.
label: none

sentence: Since we use SAC as our backbone RL algorithm, the output of the policy is naturally bounded by a squashing function (tanh), whose range is (−1, 1).
label: none

sentence: We further scale the action sampled from the Gaussian policy with a hyperparameter α, making the range of the residual action (−α, α).
label: none

sentence: We found that an appropriate scale of residual action bound can be crucial for some precise tasks.
label: none

sentence: We investigated the effects of hyperparameter α in Sec. 5.4.2.
label: none

sentence: Progressive Exploration Schedule Given that our residual policy is randomly initialized, the agent (combined with the base policy and residual policy) may exhibit highly random behavior and fail to succeed at the initial stage of learning.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, the base policy alone, trained by imitation learning, can be more reliable during the early stages.
label: none

sentence: As training progresses, the residual policy can be gradually improved, making it safer to incorporate its suggestions. 0 H Environment Steps 0.00 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 ϵ: Prob of Residual Figure 4: Progressive Explo- ration Schedule.

sentence: Inspired by the ϵ-greedy strategy used in DQN (Mnih et al., 2015), we propose to progressively introduce actions from the residual policy into the agent’s behavior policy.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, the behavior policy will use actions from the residual policy to complement the base policy with probability ϵ and rely solely on the base policy with probability 1 −ϵ.

sentence: We summarize the key details of our setups as follows (further details on the task descriptions, demonstrations, and base policy implementation can be found in Appendix A and B.1). 5.1.1 TASK DESCRIPTION Our experiments are conducted on 8 tasks across 2 benchmarks: ManiSkill (robotic manipulation; 4 tasks), and Adroit (dexterous manipulation; 4 tasks).

label: none

sentence: These complexities make it challenging for pure offline imitation learning to achieve near-perfect success rates, necessitating online learning approaches.
label: none

sentence: These demonstrations are collected by human teleoperation. 5.1.2 BASE POLICY MODEL We selected two popular imitation learning models as our base policy models for improvement.
label: none

sentence: Behavior Transformer (Shafiullah et al., 2022) is a GPT-based policy architecture for behavior cloning.
label: none

sentence: It handles multi-modal action distribution by representing an action as a combination of a cluster center (predicted by a classification head) and an offset (predicted by a regression head).
label: none

sentence: The action cluster centers are determined by k means, which is non-differentiable, thus only the offset can be fine-tuned using RL gradients.
label: none

sentence: Diffusion Policy (Chi et al., 2023) is a state-of-the-art imitation learning method that leverages recent advancements in denoising diffusion probabilistic models.
label: none

sentence: It generates robot action sequences through a conditional denoising diffusion process and employs action sequences with receding horizon control.
label: none

sentence: The training of Diffusion Policy requires ground truth action labels to supervise its denoising process; however, these action labels are unavailable in RL setups, making the original training recipe incompatible with RL.
label: none

sentence: Nevertheless, recent approaches have been developed to fine-tune diffusion models using RL in certain scenarios.

sentence: A.1.1 MANISKILL TASKS For all tasks we evaluated on ManiSkill benchmark, we use consistent setup for state space, and action space.
label: none

sentence: The state spaces adhere to a standardized template that includes proprioceptive robot state information, such as joint angles and velocities of the robot arm, and, if applicable, the mobile base.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, task-specific goal information is included within the state.
label: none

sentence: ManiSkill tasks we evaluated are very challenging because two of them require precise control and another two involve object variations.
label: none

sentence: Below, we present the key details pertaining to the tasks used in this paper.
label: none

sentence: Stack Cube • Overall Description: Pick up a red cube and place it onto a green one. • Task Difficulty: This task requires precise control.
label: none

sentence: The gripper needs to firmly grasp the red cube and accurately place it onto the green one. • Object Variations: No object variations. • Action Space: Delta position of the end-effector and joint positions of the gripper. • State Observation Space: Proprioceptive robot state information, such as joint angles and velocities of the robot arm, and task-specific goal information. • Visual Observation Space: one 64x64 RGBD image from a base camera and one 64x64 RGBD image from a hand camera.
label: none

sentence: Peg Insertion Side • Overall Description: Insert a peg into the horizontal hole in a box. • Task Difficulty: This task requires precise control.
label: none

sentence: The gripper needs to firmly grasp the peg, perfectly align it horizontally to the hole, and inserts it. • Object Variations: The box geometry is randomly generated. • Action Space: Delta pose of the end-effector and joint positions of the gripper. • State Observation Space: Proprioceptive robot state information, such as joint angles and velocities of the robot arm, and task-specific goal information. • Visual Observation Space: one 64x64 RGBD image from a base camera and one 64x64 RGBD image from a hand camera.
label: none

sentence: Turn Faucet • Overall Description: Turn on a faucet by rotating its handle. • Task Difficulty: This task needs to handle object variations.
label: none

sentence: The dataset contains trajectories of 10 faucet types, while in online interactions, the agent needs to deal with 4 novel faucets not present in the dataset.
label: none

sentence: See Fig. 12. • Object Variations: We have a source environment containing 10 faucets, and the dataset is collected in the source environment.
label: none

sentence: The agent interacts with the target environment online, which contains 4 novel faucets. • Action Space: Delta pose of the end-effector and joint positions of the gripper. • State Observation Space: Proprioceptive robot state information, such as joint angles and velocities of the robot arm, the mobile base, and task-specific goal information. 16 • Visual Observation Space: one 64x64 RGBD image from a base camera and one 64x64 RGBD image from a hand camera.
label: none

sentence: Push Chair • Overall Description: A dual-arm mobile robot needs to push a swivel chair to a target location on the ground (indicated by a red hemisphere) and prevent it from falling over.
label: none

sentence: The friction and damping parameters for the chair joints are randomized. • Task Difficulty: This task needs to handle object variations.
label: none

sentence: The dataset contains trajectories of 5 chair types, while in online interactions, the agent needs to deal with 3 novel chairs not present in the dataset.
label: none

sentence: See Fig. 12. • Object Variations: We have a source environment containing 5 chairs, and the dataset is collected in the source environment.
label: none

sentence: The agent interacts with the target environment online, which contains 3 novel chairs. • Action Space: Joint velocities of the robot arm joints and mobile robot base, and joint positions of the gripper. • State Observation Space: Proprioceptive robot state information, such as joint angles and velocities of the robot arm, task-specific goal information. • Visual Observation Space: three 50x125 RGBD images from three cameras 120◦apart from each other mounted on the robot.
label: none

sentence: Source Environment Target Environment Turn Faucet Push Chair Figure 12: For the Turn Faucet and Push Chair tasks in the ManiSkill benchmark, we have a source environment with various object instances from which the dataset is collected.

sentence: A.1.2 ADROIT TASKS Adroit Door • Overall Description: The environment is based on the Adroit manipulation platform, a 28 degree of freedom system which consists of a 24 degrees of freedom ShadowHand and a 4 degree of freedom arm.
label: none

sentence: The task to be completed consists on undoing the latch and swing the door open. • Task Difficulty: The latch has significant dry friction and a bias torque that forces the door to stay closed.
label: none

sentence: No information about the latch is explicitly provided.
label: none

sentence: The position of the door is randomized. • Object Variations: No object variations. • Action Space: Absolute angular positions of the Adroit hand joints. • State Observation Space: The angular position of the finger joints, the pose of the palm of the hand, as well as state of the latch and door. 17 • Visual Observation Space: one 128x128 RGB image from a third-person view camera.
label: none

sentence: Adroit Pen • Overall Description: The environment is based on the Adroit manipulation platform, a 28 degree of freedom system which consists of a 24 degrees of freedom ShadowHand and a 4 degree of freedom arm.
label: none

sentence: The task to be completed consists on repositioning the blue pen to match the orientation of the green target. • Task Difficulty: The target is also randomized to cover all configurations. • Object Variations: No object variations. • Action Space: Absolute angular positions of the Adroit hand joints. • State Observation Space: The angular position of the finger joints, the pose of the palm of the hand, as well as the pose of the real pen and target goal. • Visual Observation Space: one 128x128 RGB image from a third-person view camera.
label: none

sentence: Adroit Hammer • Overall Description: The environment is based on the Adroit manipulation platform, a 28 degree of freedom system which consists of a 24 degrees of freedom ShadowHand and a 4 degree of freedom arm.
label: none

sentence: The task to be completed consists on picking up a hammer with and drive a nail into a board. • Task Difficulty: The nail position is randomized and has dry friction capable of absorbing up to 15N force. • Object Variations: No object variations. • Action Space: Absolute angular positions of the Adroit hand joints. • State Observation Space: The angular position of the finger joints, the pose of the palm of the hand, the pose of the hammer and nail, and external forces on the nail. • Visual Observation Space: one 128x128 RGB image from a third-person view camera.
label: none

sentence: Adroit Relocate • Overall Description: The environment is based on the Adroit manipulation platform, a 30 degree of freedom system which consists of a 24 degrees of freedom ShadowHand and a 6 degree of freedom arm.
label: none

sentence: The task to be completed consists on moving the blue ball to the green target. • Task Difficulty: The positions of the ball and target are randomized over the entire workspace. • Object Variations: No object variations. • Action Space: Absolute angular positions of the Adroit hand joints. • State Observation Space: The angular position of the finger joints, the pose of the palm of the hand, as well as kinematic information about the ball and target. • Visual Observation Space: one 128x128 RGB image from a third-person view camera.
label: none

sentence: Note that our approach does not require such modifications, which were implemented solely for the baselines. 21 B.4.1 SAC FOR BEHAVIOR TRANSFORMER Behavior Transformer (BeT) represents an action as a combination of a cluster center (predicted by a classification head) and an offset (predicted by a regression head).
label: none

sentence: The action cluster centers are determined by k means, which is non-differentiable, thus we only fine-tune the offset using RL gradients.
label: none

sentence: Special Modifications on BeT The SAC actor network uses a tanh layer to constrain its output space to (−1, 1).
label: none

sentence: However, the offset regression head of the Behavior Transformer does not have such a bounded output space.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, we maintain the clustering process in BeT within the regular action space while adding an tanh layer to the regression head.
label: none

sentence: The Behavior Transformers used in the fine-tuning-based baselines are trained with this tanh layer.
label: none

sentence: However, due to the bounded range of the tanh function (-1, 1), certain action values cannot be represented within this range, such as gripper actions that are exactly 1.
label: none

sentence: To avoid numerical issues, we implement action rescaling.
label: none

sentence: Specifically, in ManiSkill, the gripper dimension (last action dimension) is multiplied by 0.3, while in Adroit, all actions are multiplied by 0.5.
label: none

sentence: These actions are then rescaled back to their original range after passing through the tanh function.
label: none

sentence: The modified BeT achieves similar performance in evaluations, thus enabling fair comparison.
label: none

sentence: See Table 10 for the evaluation success rates of BeT and BeT modified version in ManiSkill and Adroit tasks.
label: none

sentence: Following the general paradigm of fine-tuning GPT-based models in natural language processing, we add LoRA to all attention layers and final regression heads.
label: none

sentence: B.4.2 DIPO FOR DIFFUSION POLICY Special Modifications on DIPO DIPO employs action gradients to optimize actions and converts online training into supervised learning (more details in H.2).
label: none

sentence: While the original DIPO uses a naive diffusion model as the actor, we need to integrate DIPO with the diffusion policy.

label: none

sentence: ROT (Haldar et al., 2023a) is an online fine-tuning algorithm that fine-tunes a pre-trained base policy using behavior cloning (BC) regularization with adaptive Q-filtering and optimal transport (OT) rewards.
label: none

sentence: RLPD (Ball et al., 2023) is a state-of-the-art online learn-from-demo method that enhances the vanilla SACfd with critic layer normalization, symmetric sampling, and sample-efficient RL (Q ensemble + high UTD).
label: none

sentence: In our implementation, we maintain one offline buffer, which includes demonstration data, and one online buffer, which contains online data.
label: none

sentence: For online updates, we sample 50% batch from the offline buffer and 50% batch from the online buffer.
label: none

sentence: We omit the sample-efficient RL (Q ensemble + high UTD) due to the significant training costs associated with these components and to ensure a fair comparison with other methods.
label: limitation

label: none

sentence: Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., 2024) is an offline RL online fine-tuning method that "calibrates" the Q function of vanilla CQL.
label: none

label: none

sentence: We opted for this offline-to-online strategy because, in the online stage of the original Cal-QL paper, calculating the critic loss requires querying the actor 20 times.
label: none

label: none

label: none

sentence: Residual RL (Johannink et al., 2019) learns a residual policy in an entirely uncontrolled manner.
label: none

sentence: In our experiments, We use a pre-trained large policy as the base policy and a small MLP as the online residual actor.

sentence: F.1 OVERALL EXPLANATION Even if we have selected the strongest learning-from-demo methods, most of them are still not specifically designed for fine-tuning, and they do not intentionally prevent the unlearning of the base model, i.e., the performance can drop significantly at the very beginning of training.
label: research_gap

sentence: This phenomenon has also been discussed in Nakamoto et al. (2024).
label: none

sentence: According to our observations, we believe that performance degradation is probably due to the following two reasons: 1.
label: none

sentence: Random Critic Initialization: We believe the randomly initialized critic network cannot provide meaningful gradients to guide the policy.
label: none

sentence: Such a noisy gradient can easily cause the policy to deviate significantly from the initial weights.
label: none

sentence: Once the unlearning happens, it becomes very hard to relearn the policy since it cannot get the sparse reward signal anymore.
label: none

sentence: Sec. F.2 presents an illustrative experiment to show this policy degradation with randomly initialized critic.
label: none

sentence: On the other hand, Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., 2024) can theoretically learn a critic from offline data.
label: none

sentence: However, our empirical results indicate that when trained purely on demonstration data without negative trajectories, the learned critic does not significantly improve online fine- tuning.
label: none

sentence: This performance degradation during Cal-QL online training aligns with observations reported by (Yang et al., 2023a).
label: none

sentence: Experimental evidence supporting this analysis is presented in Sec. F.3. 2.
label: none

sentence: Long Task Horizon: Long task horizon also significantly increases the difficulty of fine-tuning, particularly in sparse reward settings.
label: none

sentence: As the task horizon increases, the agent’s likelihood of discovering sparse rewards through random exploration diminishes.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, the sparse reward signal requires more time to propagate through longer trajectories.
label: none

sentence: The experiments presented in Sec. F.4 empirically validate that the long task horizon is a key factor contributing to the failure of fine-tuning baselines.
label: none

sentence: F.2 POLICY DEGRADATION WITH RANDOM INITIALIZED CRITIC This section presents illustrative experiments demonstrating how updating the base policy with a randomly initialized critic function Q(s, a) results in significant deviations from its original trajectory.
label: none

sentence: In the StackCube task, a robot arm must pick up a red cube and stack it on a green cube.
label: none

sentence: Initially, a pre-trained base policy (Behavior Transformer) successfully grasps the red cube and accurately places it on the green cube, as shown in this video.
label: none

sentence: After fine-tuning the base policy with a randomly initialized critic for 100 gradient steps, the policy begins to deviate slightly from the original trajectory, as shown in this video.
label: none

sentence: While still able to grasp the red cube, it fails to precisely place it on the green cube.
label: none

sentence: Following an additional 100 updates (200 total), the base policy deviates further from the original trajectory, struggling to effectively grasp the red cube, as shown in this video.
label: none

sentence: In summary, these experiments suggest that fine-tuning the base policy with a randomly initialized critic can lead to unlearning.
label: none

sentence: Once unlearning occurs, it becomes very hard to relearn the policy since it cannot get the sparse reward signal anymore.
label: none

sentence: F.3 PRE-TRAINING CRITIC ON DEMO-ONLY DATASET DOES NOT HELP Cal-QL (Nakamoto et al., 2024), a state-of-the-art offline RL method, aims to pre-train a critic for efficient online fine-tuning.
label: none

sentence: Our experiments show that pre-training a critic using Cal-QL on demonstration-only datasets (without negative experiences) provides limited benefits for online 28 fine-tuning, as illustrated in Fig. 21.
label: none

sentence: This section presents experiments explaining why it does not help and validates the correctness of our Cal-QL baseline results.
label: none

sentence: The original Cal-QL paper reported much better results on Adroit tasks compared to our Cal-QL baseline.
label: none

sentence: We believe this discrepancy is mainly due to differences in experimental setups: 1.
label: none

sentence: Offline Dataset: The original Cal-QL paper uses an offline dataset consisting of 25 human teleoperation demonstrations and additional trajectories from a BC policy.
label: none

sentence: Our Cal-QL baseline uses only 25 human demonstrations, ensuring fair comparison with other learning-from-demo baselines that only utilize demonstrations.
label: none

sentence: We also made this assumption in Sec. 3. 2.
label: none

sentence: Actor Architecture: The original Cal-QL paper employs a small MLP as the actor, while we use a pre-trained Behavior Transformer (BeT) to align with our goal of improving the pre-trained base policy. 3.
label: none

sentence: Online Algorithm: The original Cal-QL paper uses Cal-QL algorithm in both offline and online stage.
label: none

sentence: However, computing critic loss in Cal-QL algorithm requires querying the actor 20 times in each update, which is extremely time-consuming given that the actor is a large model in our settings.
label: none

sentence: Therefore, we use SAC in the online phase instead of Cal-QL.
label: none

sentence: To verify whether these setup differences cause the divergent results, we designed the following experimental setups for Cal-QL, interpolating between the original setup and ours: • A: Small MLP actor + Mixed dataset + online Cal-QL (Cal-QL’s original setting) • B: Small MLP actor + Demo-only dataset + online Cal-QL • C: Small MLP actor + Demo-only dataset + online SAC • D: Large GPT actor + Demo-only dataset + online SAC • E: BeT actor + Demo-only dataset + online SAC (the setup used in our experiments) The experimental results of these setups are shown in Fig. 22.
label: none

sentence: In Cal-QL’s paper, they only report the results up to 300k steps, and our curve A perfectly matches the official results, which suggests that our implementation is correct.
label: none

sentence: Interestingly, Cal-QL exhibits instability when run for longer periods (e.g., 3M steps), even in its original setup.
label: none

sentence: Comparing curve A and curve B illustrates Cal-QL’s strong dependence on a large, diverse dataset comprising both demonstrations and negative trajectories.
label: none

sentence: Cal-QL’s sample efficiency deteriorates a lot when the offline dataset is limited to a few demonstrations without negative trajectories.
label: none

sentence: The comparison between curve B and curve C demonstrates that while using SAC as an online algorithm results in slightly reduced sample efficiency, it still achieves 90%+ success rates.
label: none

sentence: This trade-off suggests that sacrificing a little bit of sample efficiency is acceptable in exchange for significant wall-clock time savings.
label: none

sentence: The comparison between curve C and curve D illustrates that a large GPT actor can also negatively impact Cal-QL’s performance.
label: none

sentence: Curve D and curve E demonstrate that using a pre-trained BeT outperforms a randomly initialized GPT, which is expected.
label: none

sentence: In conclusion, the divergent results between Cal-QL’s original paper and our baseline can be attributed to different experimental setups.
label: none

sentence: Task Success Rate ManiSkill: TurnFaucet 0% ManiSkill: PushChair 0% Adroit: Door 0% Adroit: Pen 8% H FINE-TUNING DIFFUSION POLICY USING RL H.1 WHY FINE-TUNING DIFFUSION POLICY USING RL IS NON-TRIVIAL Diffusion Models (Ho et al., 2020) and their applications in robotic control (Chi et al., 2023; Janner et al., 2022; Ajay et al., 2022) have traditionally been trained using supervised learning, where ground truth labels (e.g., images, actions) are required to supervise the denoising process.
label: none

sentence: Recently, novel approaches (Fan & Lee, 2023; Black et al., 2023; Uehara et al., 2024) have emerged, proposing the use of reinforcement learning (RL) to train diffusion models.
label: none

sentence: The high-level idea involves modeling the denoising process as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and assigning rewards based on the quality of the final denoised samples.
label: none

sentence: This allows RL gradients to be backpropagated through the inference process, updating the model weights accordingly.
label: none

sentence: This training paradigm represents a significant departure from conventional diffusion model training methods and may face challenges when the number of denoising steps is large.
label: none

sentence: To date, these methods have primarily been applied in the domains of image generation, molecule design, and DNA synthesis.
label: none

sentence: However, this training paradigm does not directly transfer to robotic control problems, par- ticularly in sparse reward tasks.
label: research_gap

sentence: As discussed in Ren et al. (2024), fine-tuning diffusion models in robotic control can be viewed as a "two-layer" MDP, where a complete denoising process with hundreds of steps represents a single decision step in the robotic control MDP.
label: none

sentence: For example, if a robotic task requires 200 decision steps (actions) to complete, and a diffusion model uses 100 denoising steps to generate a decision (action), the reward in a sparse-reward robotic control task would be received only every 20,000 denoising steps.
label: none

sentence: This presents a significantly greater challenge than training a diffusion model to generate images using RL, where rewards are typically received every 100 denoising steps under the same assumptions.
label: none

sentence: H.2 HOW "BASIC RL FOR DIFFUSION POLICY" BASELINE IS SELECTED Despite the challenges in training diffusion policies for robotic control using RL, recent attempts have emerged.
label: none

sentence: These can be broadly grouped into three categories.
label: none

sentence: We will briefly explain each method and discuss the selection of the "Basic RL" baseline for fine-tuning diffusion policy. 33 Converting RL into Supervised Learning Methods in this category adhere to the conventional training recipe of the diffusion models, and try to define a "ground truth action label" for supervision.
label: none

sentence: DIPO (Yang et al., 2023b) introduces "action gradient," using gradient descent on Q(s, a) to estimate the optimal action for state s.
label: none

sentence: DIPO is selected as the basic RL algorithm in our experiments.
label: none

sentence: IDQL (Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023) constructs an implicit policy by reweighting samples from a diffusion-based policy, and using the implicit policy to supervise the training of the diffusion-based policy.
label: none

sentence: We did not select it as the fine-tuning baseline for two reasons: 1) the training can be extremely slow especially with large base policies, because IDQL involves sampling the diffusion model multiple times (32 to 128 in their code) to compute the implicit policy; 2) as reported in its paper, IDQL performs worse than Cal-QL and RLPD, which are included in our baselines.
label: none

sentence: Matching the Score to the Q Function QSM (Psenka et al., 2023) aims to match the score Ψ of the diffusion-based policy to the gradient of the Q function ∇aQΨ(s, a) using supervised learning.
label: none

sentence: According to Ren et al. (2024), QSM performs poorly in robotic manipulation tasks, thus it is not considered a competitive baseline.
label: none

sentence: Backpropagating RL Gradients Through the Inference Process Methods in this category adapt the training recipe discussed in H.1 to robotic control tasks, employing additional techniques to make it work.
label: none

sentence: The actor’s training objective is to maximize Q(s, a).
label: none

sentence: Diffusion QL (Wang et al., 2022) represents a basic version of these methods, primarily used in offline RL settings.
label: none

sentence: However, its online performance is poor, as reported by Ren et al. (2024).
label: none

sentence: Consistency AC (Ding & Jin, 2023) distills diffusion models into consistency models, significantly shortening the gradient propagation path.
label: none

sentence: Nevertheless, its offline-to-online performance, as reported in its own paper, is even worse than Diffusion QL, thus we do not consider it a competitive baseline.
label: none

sentence: DPPO (Ren et al., 2024), a very recent work, successfully fine-tunes diffusion policies using PPO, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
label: none

sentence: Key tricks include fine-tuning only the last few denoising steps and fine-tuning DDIM sampling.
label: none

sentence: We conducted preliminary experiments comparing our approach with DPPO on their tasks.
label: none

sentence: Results indicate that our method significantly outperforms DPPO on their tasks.
label: none

sentence: See Appendix C.1 for more details.
label: none

sentence: Re- markably, we show that a simple triplet loss outperforms state-of-the-art methods, suggesting that much of the improvements in recent approaches could be attributed to differences in data and architectures. 1 INTRODUCTION The increasing momentum of embodied intelligence has motivated the study of generalizable re- ward models that do not rely on hand-crafted human supervision.
label: none

sentence: Recent work leverages large vision-language models (VLMs) as general-purpose reward functions that measure progress through alignment between visual observations and language goals.
label: none

sentence: Rocamonde et al. (2024) showed that CLIP (Radford et al., 2021) can be used as a zero-shot reward model for downstream policy learn- ing, though it struggles with domain shift related to action specification and environmental dynam- ics.
label: research_gap

sentence: To mitigate this effect, many methods have turned to large-scale video demonstration datasets (Damen et al., 2018; Grauman et al., 2022) to finetune VLMs, enabling a better understanding of task-relevant behaviors.
label: none

sentence: Nevertheless, the question of extracting meaningful signals of task progress from video demonstrations remains a central challenge to vision-language reward modeling.
label: research_gap

sentence: As a result, increasingly complex learning objectives have been proposed to generate more accurate rewards (Sermanet et al., 2018; Nair et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023b;a; Karamcheti et al., 2023).
label: none

sentence: How- ever, most of these methods were pre-trained using different datasets and architectures, making it difficult to isolate the choice of learning objective from downstream performance.
label: research_gap

sentence: LIV (Ma et al., 2023a) was initialized with CLIP weights and pre-trained on EpicKitchen (Nair et al., 2022) yet compares to methods utilizing a frozen BERT encoder Devlin et al. (2019) and vision encoder pre-trained on Ego4D from scratch (Nair et al., 2022).

sentence: We assess model performance via two distinct benchmarks, evaluating consistency with ground truth reward and alignment with expert progress.

sentence: Limit Theorems for Stochastic Gradient Descent with Infinite Variance Jose Blanchet1, Aleksandar Mijatović2, and Wenhao Yang1 1Management Science and Engineering, Stanford University 2Department of Statistics, University of Warwick September 9, 2025 Abstract Stochastic gradient descent is a classic algorithm that has gained great popularity especially in the last decades as the most common approach for training models in machine learning.
label: none

sentence: While the algorithm has been well-studied when stochastic gradients are assumed to have a finite variance, there is significantly less research addressing its theoretical properties in the case of infinite variance gradients.
label: research_gap

sentence: In this paper, we establish the asymptotic behavior of stochastic gradient descent in the context of infinite variance stochastic gradients, assuming that the stochastic gradient is regular varying with index α ∈(1, 2).
label: none

sentence: The closest result in this context was established in 1969 [26], in the one-dimensional case and assuming that stochastic gradients belong to a more restrictive class of distributions.
label: none

sentence: We extend it to the multidimensional case, covering a broader class of infinite variance distributions.
label: none

sentence: As we show, the asymptotic distribution of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm can be characterized as the stationary distribution of a suitably defined Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process driven by an appropriate stable Lévy process.
label: none

sentence: Additionally, we explore the applications of these results in linear regression and logistic regression models. 1 Introduction Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) and its variants constitute a class of algorithms rooted in stochastic approximation methods [24, 41] and have demonstrated significant success in training models for various machine learning applications [11, 25].
label: none

sentence: This empirical success has motivated extensive research into the theoretical properties of SGD, including finite-sample and asymptotic analyses, as well as algorithmic improvements [6, 27, 34–37, 42].
label: none

sentence: However, most of these advancements assume stochastic gradients with finite variance.
label: research_gap

sentence: In this work, we aim to extend the theoretical understanding of SGD by examining its behavior under stochastic gradients with infinite variance.
label: none

sentence: To set the stage for this investigation, we first review the standard formulation of SGD.
label: none

sentence: Consider the following problem: min θ∈Rd Eξ∼P [ℓ(θ, ξ)], where ξ : Ω→E is a random variable on probability space (Ω, P, F) and ℓ: Rd × E →R is a strongly convex function.
label: none

sentence: The SGD algorithm is an iterative scheme to find the near optimal solution θ∗∈argminθ∈Rd Eξ∼P [ℓ(θ, ξ)]: θn+1 = θn −ηn∇ℓ(θn, ξn+1), (1) where {ξn}n≥1 is an i.i.d. sequence, E[∇ℓ(θn, ξn+1)|σ(ξ1, · · · , ξn)] = Eξ∼P [∇ℓ(θn, ξ)] and ηn is the learning rate.
label: none

sentence: It is worth noticing if ∇ℓ(θ, ξ) is replaced with a general function H(θ, ξ), the iteration (1) becomes the standard stochastic approximation procedure [41] for solving the equation EH(θ, ξ) = 0.
label: none

sentence: From a statistical inference perspective, analyzing the limiting behavior of the estimator θn is crucial for uncertainty quantification, such as constructing confidence intervals that support reliable decision- making.

sentence: When the stochastic gradient ∇ℓ(θ, ξ) has finite variance, it can be shown [28, 43] that the 1 arXiv:2410.16340v4 [stat.ML] 5 Sep 2025 asymptotic distribution of θn satisfies: q η−1 n (θn −θ∗) ⇒N(0, Σ), where the asymptotic variance Σ satisfies the Lyapunov equation: E[∇2ℓ(θ∗, ξ)]Σ + ΣE[∇2ℓ(θ∗, ξ)] = Γ, and Γ = Cov(∇ℓ(θ∗, ξ), ∇ℓ(θ∗, ξ)).
label: none

sentence: It can also be equivalently shown [5, 37] the asymptotic distribution is the stationary distribution of the following stochastic differential equation: dZt = −E[∇2ℓ(θ∗, ξ)]Ztdt + Γ 1 2 dBt, which is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process driven by a Brownian motion process.

sentence: Recently, a complementary line of work has emerged on high-dimensional scaling limits of SGD and related online learning algorithms, where the dimension grows with the sample size (e.g., [2, 4, 48]).

sentence: These studies typically assume finite-variance noise and analyze the limiting dynamics via PDE, mean-field, or weak convergence techniques, revealing rich phase-transition phenomena governed by the step-size, dimension, and number of steps.

sentence: This phenomenon arises from the multiplication of many random weights during backpropagation via the chain rule, where some of these random weights can occasionally be expansive.
